task: Edit this fictional patient-booklet passage to 55–85 words, followed by one AMA 11 reference. Keep an understandable attribution to the clinic's survey article as well as its number: a bare number is not enough for this audience. Restore the consent quotation exactly. The venue uses [1] after punctuation as a plain-text superscript surrogate. Reference format: Author initials. Article title. Journal abbreviation. Year;volume(issue):pages. The journal abbreviation and all available fields are supplied. Do not turn preference responses into a health outcome or add advice about care.
input:
The Sedgewick Clinic survey proves that everyone needs reminders by phone. You must answer every question before your appointment. The article says, “Skipping a question may affect your appointment.”[1]

1. Ula Dray; Tomi Vesk. Choosing a reminder channel. Patient Forms Review, 2023.

facts.text: The Sedgewick Clinic survey article describes reminder preferences among 30 people who chose to answer its questionnaire; 18 selected phone reminders.
The article's consent statement is exactly “Skipping a question will not affect your appointment.”
The survey measured preferences, not clinical outcomes, and did not establish the preferences of people who did not respond.
Article record: Ula Dray and Tomi Vesk; Choosing a reminder channel; journal abbreviation Patient Forms Rev; 2023; volume 5; issue 3; pages 81–86.

forbidden_additions: A requirement to complete the survey to obtain an appointment
A claim that phone reminders improve health or suit every patient
Invented DOI, publication fields, or medical recommendations
preserve: Skipping a question will not affect your appointment.
Patient-friendly attribution to the Sedgewick Clinic survey article
18 of the 30 voluntary respondents selected phone reminders
